# Git and GitHub for Solo Developers {#sec-git-solo}

In March you write the cleaning script for a readmissions
analysis, and it excludes patients with implausible blood
pressures. In November a reviewer asks why 212 patients were
excluded when the protocol implies fewer, and the person who must
answer is you, eight months and three projects later, with no
memory of the decision. Without a history, the answer is a
reconstruction from memory and from files named
`clean_final2.R`. With Git it is one command,
`git log -p R/clean.R`, which shows when the exclusion rule
changed, what it changed from, and, if the March analyst wrote a
good commit message, why. You are not one person over the life of
a project, and the collaboration Git supports is real: it is
asynchronous, and it is with yourself.

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat
it.*

[George Santayana]{.smallcaps}, *The Life of Reason* (1905)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

**You'll need.** @sec-shell for the command line, and
@sec-workstation for Git installed and configured with your name
and email. Every command in this chapter runs in a shell, not in
R, so the examples are display-only; the exercises build a
throwaway practice repository, and each solution gives the output
to expect.

**You'll be able to.**

- Make commits that each record one logical change with a
  message that says why, and read the history back with
  `git log`.
- Experiment on a branch, merge it, and resolve a merge conflict.
- Push to a private GitHub repository over SSH or with a token,
  and tag the commit you submit.
- Recover from the common mistakes, choosing the command that
  destroys nothing first.

## Why one analyst needs a history {#sec-git-solo-why}

Nearly every argument for version control is an argument about
collaboration: merging other people's work, reviewing their
changes, avoiding the overwrite of a file two people edited at
once. None of that applies to an analyst working alone, which is
why solo Git is a harder sell than it looks, and why many
statisticians postpone learning it until a project forces the
issue.

The case for solo use rests on the March and November analysts.
Everything Git offers a team it offers to that pair, and each of
November's questions has a Git answer (@tbl-git-solo-why).

| November's question | What answers it | Command |
|---|---|---|
| When did this number change, and why? | The commit history and its messages | `git log -p R/clean.R` |
| Exactly what did we submit? | A tag on the submitted commit | `git switch --detach v1.0-submission` |
| Can I try a risky change without endangering the analysis of record? | A branch | `git switch -c sensitivity` |
| What if the laptop dies? | A copy on a remote server | `git push` |
| The project now has a second analyst | Nothing new: the history and the remote already exist | @sec-git-teams |

: What Git gives one analyst. {#tbl-git-solo-why}

The cost is a few hours of learning and a few seconds per commit.
The benefit recurs on every project for the rest of your career,
and many 'solo' projects become team projects, at which point a
repository that already exists is the difference between sharing
code in an afternoon and scrambling for a week.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You keep dated copies of the project folder
(`analysis_2026-03-14/`, `analysis_2026-04-02/`). What does that
give the November analyst, and what does it not?

**Answer.** It records *when*, coarsely, and lets you recover a
whole folder. It does not record *what* changed (you must diff
folders by hand), *why* it changed (there is no message), or which
copy was submitted (unless you remember the date). It also makes
experiments expensive, since each one is another full copy, and
nothing stops you from editing an old copy by mistake. A commit
records a line-level change with a reason; a tag names the
submitted state; a branch makes an experiment free.
:::

## The everyday cycle {#sec-git-solo-cycle}

On most days, Git is five commands: look, compare, stage, commit,
repeat (display-only, as is every command in this chapter).

```bash
# once per project
cd ~/research/my-project
git init -b main
git add .
git commit -m "Initial project structure"

# day to day
git status
git diff
git add R/clean.R
git commit -m "Exclude SBP above 280 mmHg, per SAP section 6.2"
git log --oneline -10
```

`git diff` shows changes you have not yet staged; `git diff
--staged` shows what the next commit will contain. The
distinction is between 'I have edited this' and 'I have marked
this for the next commit', and the second command is the one to
read before every commit.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**`git add .` stages whatever is in the directory.** On an analysis
project that is routinely more than you meant: a rendered PDF, a
cache directory, a data extract you are not licensed to
redistribute, an `.Renviron` holding a database password. Git has
no opinion about any of it. Read `git status` before staging, list
derived and secret files in `.gitignore`, and consider a secret
scanner such as `gitleaks` as a pre-commit hook.[^zzgit] A
credential that reaches a pushed commit must be treated as
compromised and rotated, even after the file is deleted, because
the old commit still contains it.
:::

[^zzgit]: One way to automate part of this is the in-house `zzgit`
    zsh plugin (@sec-lab-software), which wraps staging and
    committing with a prompt for a Conventional Commits subject
    line and a confirmation before pushing to a protected branch.
    Content scanning requires `gitleaks` to be installed separately;
    without it, `zzgit` falls back to a filename check only and will
    commit a secret in a file like `.Renviron` without warning, and
    the protected-branch confirmation guards a push, not a commit.
    Install `gitleaks` as a pre-commit hook, with or without
    `zzgit`, for the content scan itself. `zzgit` is optional; the
    habit it enforces is not.

### Commits as units of reasoning

Git's commands can be memorized in a week. What distinguishes a
repository that answers questions from one that merely stores
files is two habits the commands do not enforce.

**Each commit is one logical change.** 'Refactor data cleaning to
use vectorized assignment' is a commit; 'Tuesday's work' is not.
Atomic commits make `git bisect`, the binary search for the commit
that introduced a bug (@sec-git-teams), feasible; large commits
make it useless.

**The message says why.** The diff already shows what changed;
only the message can say why (@tbl-git-solo-messages, in which
SAP is the statistical analysis plan of @sec-analysis-plan).

| A message that says what | A message that says why |
|---|---|
| update SEs | Switch to HC1 sandwich standard errors: residual plots show heteroscedasticity |
| fix filter | Exclude SBP above 280 mmHg, per SAP section 6.2 |
| changes | Drop site E visits before 2024-03: export bug confirmed by data manager |
| Tuesday's work | (Three commits, one per change) |

: Commit messages for the November analyst. {#tbl-git-solo-messages}

A useful test is to write the message first. If it needs the word
'and', or a list of unrelated items, the commit is doing too much.

`git log` has many options; the useful subset is short.

```bash
git log --oneline -10
git log --grep "bootstrap"
git log -p R/clean.R
git log --since="2 weeks ago"
```

These show, in order, the last ten commits one line each, the
commits whose message mentions 'bootstrap', every change ever
made to one file with its diff, and recent activity.

### Exercises

1. Build the practice repository the rest of this chapter's
   exercises use. In an empty directory (for example
   `~/git-practice`), run the commands below, then run
   `git status` and `git log --oneline`. What do they print?

```bash
git init -b main
printf '# HF-HOME practice\n' > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m 'Add README'
mkdir R
printf 'visits <- read.csv("visits.csv")\nthreshold <- 250\n' > R/clean.R
git add R/clean.R
git commit -m 'Read visits as exported'
printf 'stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(visits$visit_id))\n' >> R/clean.R
git commit -am 'Assert one row per visit'
```

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
`git status` prints `On branch main` and `nothing to commit,
working tree clean`. `git log --oneline` prints three lines,
newest first; your seven-character hashes will differ, because a
hash depends on the author, time, and content:

```
fb2dbac Assert one row per visit
37c6e4f Read visits as exported
94a17b3 Add README
```

The last commit used `git commit -am`, which stages every change
to a file Git already tracks and commits it in one step. It does
not pick up new files, which is why the first two commits needed
`git add`. If `git log` shows fewer commits, run `git status`: a
commit that failed for want of a configured name and email
(@sec-workstation) leaves the change staged.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In one morning you cleaned the data, fixed a typo in
the README, fitted three candidate models, and deleted an old
script. How many commits is that, and what is the test?

**Answer.** Several, and the test is whether you could revert one
part without losing the others. Cleaning the data, fixing the
README, and deleting the script are three unrelated intentions;
bundled together, discovering next week that the cleaning rule was
wrong means reverting the README fix too. The three model fits
depend on intent: if they are alternatives you are choosing
between, commit each, so that you can point at the one you kept;
if they are one specification search you always meant to run
together, they are one commit. This matters more in solo work than
it seems, because you are the only reviewer you will ever get.
:::

## Branches and merges {#sec-git-solo-branches}

A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. Creating a branch makes
a new pointer, and the branch moves forward as you commit on it.
@fig-git-branch shows the shape a solo analyst's history tends to
take: a main line carrying the trustworthy analysis, with
short-lived branches for experiments that are merged back if they
work out and abandoned if they do not.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-git-branch
%%| fig-alt: "Git commit graph. The main line runs through commits
%%|   for initializing the compendium, cleaning data, and fitting
%%|   the primary model. A sensitivity-analysis branch splits off
%%|   after data cleaning, gains two commits for an MNAR sensitivity
%%|   analysis and a tipping-point analysis, then merges back into
%%|   main. A final manuscript commit is tagged submitted-v1."
%%| fig-cap: "A solo analyst's branch history. The main line carries
%%|   the analysis of record and is tagged at submission; a
%%|   sensitivity-analysis branch explores an alternative and is merged
%%|   only once it is trusted."
gitGraph
  commit id: "init compendium"
  commit id: "clean data"
  branch sensitivity-analysis
  checkout sensitivity-analysis
  commit id: "MNAR sensitivity"
  commit id: "tipping point"
  checkout main
  commit id: "primary model"
  merge sensitivity-analysis
  commit id: "manuscript" tag: "submitted-v1"
```

The commands that produce such a history:

```bash
git switch -c sensitivity-analysis
git add R/sensitivity.R
git commit -m "Add sensitivity analysis under MNAR"
git switch main
git merge sensitivity-analysis
git branch -d sensitivity-analysis
```

`git switch -c` creates a branch and moves to it; `git switch
main` moves back; `git merge` brings the branch's commits into
the current branch; `git branch -d` deletes a branch whose work
has been merged.[^switch] MNAR (missing not at random) is the
kind of sensitivity analysis a solo analyst most often wants to
try without committing to it (@sec-missing).

[^switch]: `git switch` and `git restore` arrived in Git 2.23
    (2019) to split the many jobs of `git checkout`, which still
    works and appears in older guides.

For solo work, branches suit three kinds of work: experiments you
might throw away, such as a risky refactor; side investigations,
such as a sensitivity analysis you may or may not report; and
separable pieces of a longer project. The discipline is to keep
`main` working at all times. If a branch is half-done, leave it on
its branch.

`git rebase` is an alternative to `merge` that produces a linear
history. For solo work the difference rarely matters; pick one and
use it consistently. `merge` is simpler to reason about.

### When a merge conflicts

If the branch and `main` both changed the same lines, Git cannot
choose and stops with a *merge conflict*. It writes both versions
into the file between markers:

```
visits <- read.csv("visits.csv")
<<<<<<< HEAD
threshold <- 280
=======
threshold <- 300
>>>>>>> sbp-300
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(visits$visit_id))
```

The lines between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` are the current
branch's version; those between `=======` and `>>>>>>> sbp-300`
are the incoming branch's. Resolving the conflict means editing
the file to the content you intend, which may be either side,
both, or neither, deleting all three marker lines, then
`git add R/clean.R` and `git commit --no-edit`, which records the
merge with Git's default message. For analysis code, both sides
usually represent deliberate decisions: here one is the SAP's
threshold and the other a sensitivity analysis, and the right
resolution keeps the SAP value in the primary script and moves the
alternative to its own script, not a coin toss between them.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Before committing a resolution, confirm that no markers remain
anywhere in the tracked files, then rerun the analysis:

```bash
git grep -n -e '<<<<<<<' -e '>>>>>>>'
```

No output means no markers. A marker left in an R script stops
the script with a parse error; a marker left in a CSV or a
Markdown file is read as data or text without complaint.
:::

### Exercises

2. In the practice repository, plant and resolve a conflict.
   Create a branch `sbp-300` and set `threshold <- 300` in
   `R/clean.R`; commit. Switch to `main` and set
   `threshold <- 280`; commit. Merge `sbp-300`, resolve the
   conflict in favor of 280, and commit. What does
   `git log --oneline --graph` print?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
One way to make each edit without an editor is to rewrite the
file whole, as here for the branch (use 280 on `main`):

```bash
printf '%s\n' 'visits <- read.csv("visits.csv")' \
  'threshold <- 300' \
  'stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(visits$visit_id))' > R/clean.R
```

The merge prints `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in R/clean.R`,
and `git status --short` marks the file `UU`. After the resolution
and `git commit --no-edit`, the graph shows the two lines of work
meeting at the merge commit (your hashes and the order of the two
middle commits may differ):

```
*   11d6d7e Merge branch 'sbp-300'
|\
| * 2853126 Raise SBP threshold to 300 for sensitivity
* | 93d5df5 Set SBP threshold to 280 per SAP
|/
* fb2dbac Assert one row per visit
* 37c6e4f Read visits as exported
* 94a17b3 Add README
```

`cat R/clean.R` shows `threshold <- 280` and no marker lines.
Delete the merged branch with `git branch -d sbp-300`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A merge completes with no conflict. Does that mean
the merged analysis is correct?

**Answer.** No. Git detects only overlapping edits to the same
lines. If the branch renamed a variable in one file and `main`
added a use of the old name in another, the merge is clean and the
script fails, or, worse, finds a stale object and runs. Rerun the
analysis after every merge. @sec-git-teams returns to these
semantic conflicts, which become common once two people share a
repository.
:::

## Remotes and authentication {#sec-git-solo-remotes}

A remote is a copy of the repository hosted elsewhere. GitHub is
the dominant choice; GitLab is similar, and Gitea is a self-hosted
alternative. Even for solo work, a remote is your off-site backup:
a laptop fire ends a project that was never pushed, and is a
setback for one that was.

```bash
gh repo create my-analysis --private --source=. --remote=origin
git push -u origin main

git push
git pull
```

The first line creates a private repository with the GitHub
command-line tool `gh` and registers it as the remote `origin`.
The `-u origin main` on the first push sets the upstream, so that
later `git push` and `git pull` need no arguments. Make
repositories public deliberately, never by accident; a private
repository costs nothing.

GitHub stopped accepting account passwords for Git operations in
2021, so you authenticate in one of two ways.

| Method | Setup | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Personal access token (PAT) | Create a fine-grained token in your GitHub settings, limited to the repositories it needs, with an expiration date; or let `gh auth login` create and store one | You want the fastest start, or you work over HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) |
| SSH (Secure Shell) key | `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"`, then add the public key with `gh ssh-key add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` or in your GitHub settings | You push often from one machine; clone with `git@github.com:user/repo.git` URLs |

: Authenticating to GitHub. {#tbl-git-solo-auth}

Either works; `gh auth login` handles the common case for both.
GitHub's settings menus move from time to time, so if a path in
its documentation has changed, search for 'personal access token'
or 'SSH keys'.

### Exercises

3. Create a private GitHub repository for the practice repository
   and push `main` to it. How do you confirm, from the shell, that
   the remote has your latest commit?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
From inside the repository, `gh repo create git-practice --private
--source=. --remote=origin` followed by `git push -u origin main`.
Then `git status` should include
`Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'`, and the hash
`git ls-remote origin main` prints should equal the one
`git rev-parse main` prints. `git status` compares against the
last state Git fetched; `git ls-remote` asks the server now, which
is the stronger check. Delete the practice repository on GitHub
when you finish the chapter (`gh repo delete git-practice`, which
needs the `delete_repo` scope).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You pushed a commit that added `.Renviron` with a
database password to a private repository, then deleted the file
in the next commit. Is the password safe?

**Answer.** No. The earlier commit still contains the file, and
anyone with access to the repository, now or after it is made
public or shared with a collaborator, can read it with
`git show <hash>:.Renviron`. Rotate the password first; that is
the step that protects the database. Removing the file from history
requires rewriting it and force-pushing, which does not reach
copies already cloned.
:::

## Tags and detached HEAD {#sec-git-solo-tags}

A tag is an immovable, named pointer to a commit. Tag the moments
you may need to return to exactly: submission to a journal, each
round of revision (`v1.1-revision-1`), the published version, and
internal milestones such as results sent to the principal
investigator (PI).

```bash
git tag -a v1.0 -m "Submitted to Journal of Biostatistics 2026-04"
git push origin v1.0
git tag
git switch --detach v1.0
git switch main
```

The `-a` makes an annotated tag, which records who tagged, when,
and a message; prefer it to a lightweight tag. Tags are not pushed
by `git push` alone, so push each one by name. Once a tag is
pushed, treat it as permanent.

### Detached HEAD

`git switch --detach v1.0` (or the older `git checkout v1.0`) puts
the repository in a *detached HEAD* state: you are on a commit,
not on a branch. Looking around, rerunning, and rendering are all
safe. A commit made there belongs to no branch, and it drops out
of view when you switch away. To build on a tagged version, create
a branch from it first: `git switch -c revision-1 v1.0`.

This is how you answer the reviewer who asks, six months later,
for a rerun with the original exclusion criterion: switch to the
submission tag, rerun, compare with `main`, and switch back. The
tag is the record of which version was reported.

### Exercises

4. Tag the current commit of the practice repository as
   `v1.0-submission`, with a message. What does
   `git log --oneline --decorate -1` print? Then switch to the tag
   with `--detach`: what is the first line of `git status`?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
After `git tag -a v1.0-submission -m 'Submitted to journal'`, the
log line carries both pointers:

```
11d6d7e (HEAD -> main, tag: v1.0-submission) Merge branch 'sbp-300'
```

After `git switch --detach v1.0-submission`, `git status` begins
`HEAD detached at v1.0-submission`. Return with `git switch main`.
If you pushed the repository in Exercise 3, push the tag with
`git push origin v1.0-submission`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You have committed and pushed your finished analysis.
Why also tag the commit?

**Answer.** A commit hash such as `a3f9c8d` is unmemorable and
looks like every other hash; in two years you will not know which
one you submitted. The tag `v1.0-submission` is human-readable,
records when and why it was made, and appears in the repository's
list of tags on GitHub. A GitHub *Release* is a separate object
built on a tag, with notes and attached files, and exists only if
you create one (`gh release create v1.0-submission`).
:::

## Recovery {#sec-git-solo-recovery}

Most Git mistakes can be undone, and the first move is almost
always one that destroys nothing. @tbl-git-solo-oh-no lists the
common ones in the form you will meet them.

| Oh no, I... | Run | Destroys anything? |
|---|---|---|
| edited a file and want the committed version back | `git restore R/clean.R` | Yes: your uncommitted edits to that file |
| staged a file I did not mean to | `git restore --staged R/clean.R` | No |
| wrote a bad message on the last commit (not yet pushed) | `git commit --amend -m "Better message"` | No |
| committed too early and want the changes back (not yet pushed) | `git reset --soft HEAD~1` | No: the changes stay staged |
| committed to `main` instead of a new branch (not yet pushed) | `git branch topic`, then `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, then `git switch topic` | No, if the working tree was clean first |
| pushed a commit that was wrong | `git revert <hash>` | No: a new commit undoes it |
| ran `git reset --hard` and lost commits | `git reflog`, then `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` | No, if the reflog shows the commit |
| committed while in detached HEAD | `git switch -c rescue` before switching away; afterward, find it in `git reflog` | No |
| need to switch branches with unfinished work | `git commit` on the branch, or `git stash` | No |
| pushed a secret | Rotate the credential first; then see the Check in @sec-git-solo-remotes | The secret is already exposed |

: The 'Oh no, I...' table. Run `git status` before and after each
fix. {#tbl-git-solo-oh-no}

### The commands behind the table

`git reset` moves the current branch to another commit. Its three
modes differ only in what happens to the changes the move skips
over.

```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git reset HEAD~1
git reset --hard HEAD~1
```

The first undoes the last commit and keeps its changes staged; the
second keeps them unstaged; the third discards them. `HEAD~1`
means 'one commit before the current one'.

`git reflog` lists every move of `HEAD` in your local repository,
including the ones `reset` hides from `git log`. Commits that no
branch reaches remain listed there for 30 days by default (the
`gc.reflogExpireUnreachable` setting), and entries for commits
still on a branch for 90 days. It is the recovery mechanism of
last resort: if you deleted a commit in a panic, the reflog
probably still has it.

`git stash` sets uncommitted work aside so that you can switch
branches, and `git stash pop` brings it back. Prefer a commit for
work that matters: a popped or dropped stash leaves the reflog,
and survives only as an unreachable object that
`git fsck --no-reflogs --unreachable` lists until garbage
collection prunes it, typically after two weeks.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**`git reset --hard` deletes uncommitted work, and nothing brings
it back.** The reflog records commits, not edits you never
committed. Before any command marked 'Yes' in
@tbl-git-solo-oh-no, run `git status`; if anything you want is
listed, commit it (on a scratch branch if need be) first.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Recovery is where a model's first suggestion is most often
destructive. Give it the evidence and forbid the shortcut.

> **Context.** Below are the output of `git status`,
> `git log --oneline --graph -15`, and `git reflog -15` for my
> analysis repository. What went wrong: [I ran `git reset --hard`
> and the commit 'Fit primary model' is gone from `git log`].
>
> **Constraints.** Use the reflog before anything else. Propose no
> `reset --hard`, `clean -f`, `push --force`, or `restore .` unless
> you first give a command that preserves the current state (a
> branch or a commit). Explain what each command does before I run
> it.
>
> **Criteria.** After your commands, `git log --oneline` shows the
> lost commit, `git status` shows nothing I had before is lost, and
> you state which reflog entry you used.

*Failure mode.* The model reaches for `git reset --hard` or
`git push --force` first, which on a tree with uncommitted work
destroys exactly what the reflog cannot restore. A coding agent
with a shell adds a second risk: it may run the command before you
read it. Before any agent session that can edit the repository,
commit, or start a branch (`git switch -c agent/<task>`), so that
`git diff main` shows everything the agent did and
`git switch main` abandons it. *Check.* Run the three criteria
commands yourself. Status, log, and reflog output hold file names
and messages, not data, so they may go to any approved tool; read
the messages for identifiers first (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

### Exercises

5. In the practice repository, commit a new line
   (`printf 'n_visits <- nrow(visits)\n' >> R/clean.R`, then
   `git commit -am 'Count visits'`), destroy the commit with
   `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, and recover it. Which reflog entry
   do you use, and how do you confirm the recovery?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
`git reflog -2` shows the reset on top and the lost commit one
entry below it:

```
11d6d7e HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
aa1302f HEAD@{1}: commit: Count visits
```

`git reset --hard 'HEAD@{1}'` restores it (the quotes stop some
shells from expanding the braces). `git log --oneline -1` then
prints `aa1302f Count visits` (your hash differs), and
`tail -n 1 R/clean.R` prints the restored line. `--hard` is safe
here only because `git status` was clean before the reset.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Which of these can the reflog recover: (a) a commit
removed by `git reset --hard`; (b) edits you made and never
committed, then discarded with `git restore`; (c) a commit on a
branch you deleted with `git branch -D` last week?

**Answer.** (a) and (c): both were commits, and the reflog records
every commit `HEAD` has visited for at least 30 days. (b) cannot be
recovered by Git at all, because Git never saw the edits; only an
editor's undo history or a backup can help. This asymmetry is the
practical argument for committing early and often.
:::

## Worked example: a solo project lifecycle {#sec-git-solo-worked}

The lifecycle below is display-only. It shows when each command
runs over the life of one project.

```bash
# day 1: start the project
mkdir ~/research/readmissions && cd ~/research/readmissions
git init -b main
echo "# Readmissions analysis" > README.md
printf '%s\n' '*.html' '*.pdf' '.Rproj.user/' '.Rhistory' \
  '.RData' '.Renviron' > .gitignore
git add . && git commit -m "Initial structure"
gh repo create readmissions --private --source=. --remote=origin
git push -u origin main

# week 2: data exploration
git add R/01_explore.R
git commit -m "Initial EDA, summarizing 30-day rates"

# week 4: try a sensitivity analysis on a branch
git switch -c sensitivity-mnar
git add R/03_sensitivity.R
git commit -m "MNAR sensitivity by IPW"
git switch main
git merge sensitivity-mnar
git branch -d sensitivity-mnar

# week 8: submit
git tag -a v1.0-jbs-submission -m "Submitted to JBS 2026-06-15"
git push origin v1.0-jbs-submission

# week 22: revision request
git diff v1.0-jbs-submission main --stat
git switch --detach v1.0-jbs-submission
# rerun, compare with current main, decide what to change
git switch main
git tag -a v1.1-jbs-revision-1 -m "First revision JBS"
git push origin v1.1-jbs-revision-1
```

The `.gitignore` written on day 1 keeps rendered output, editor
state, the saved workspace, and the secrets file out of every
later `git add .`. The branch kept the sensitivity work, an
inverse probability weighting (IPW) analysis, isolated until it
was ready. The tags make the timeline navigable, and the remote is
the off-site backup if the laptop dies.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that the history has the shape you intended and that the
server holds your tags:

```bash
git log --oneline --decorate --graph -10
git ls-remote --tags origin
```

The first shows each tag beside its commit; the second lists the
tags on GitHub. A tag that appears in the first and not the second
was never pushed.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In week 22, why switch to the tag with `--detach`
rather than reset `main` to it?

**Answer.** Because the goal is to look, not to move. `--detach`
leaves `main`, and every commit made since submission, exactly
where it is; switching back restores the current state. Resetting
`main` to the tag would move the branch backward and hide the
post-submission work from `git log`, recoverable only through the
reflog.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 3: version control from day one.** One logical change
   per commit, a message that says why, and a push to a private
   remote at the end of each day.
2. **Habit 5: pre-specify, then tag.** Tag every irreversible
   moment (the analysis plan, each submission, results sent to the
   PI), so that 'what exactly did we report?' has an answer.
3. **Habit 12: every model output is a hypothesis until verified.**
   Commit or branch before an agent touches the repository, and
   prefer the recovery command that destroys nothing.

## Cumulative practice

6. *Cumulative (uses @sec-shell and @sec-why).* In the practice
   repository, add a `.gitignore` that excludes `output/` and
   `.Renviron`, create `output/table1.csv` and an `.Renviron`
   with any content, and commit with `git add .`. Then tag the
   commit `v1.1-compendium`. Which files did the commit contain?
7. *On your own work (no key).* Put a current project under Git
   with a `.gitignore` written before the first `git add`, push it
   to a private remote, and tag the last version you sent to
   anyone.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
`git show --stat v1.1-compendium` lists `.gitignore` alone:
`output/table1.csv` and `.Renviron` were ignored, and
`git status --ignored` lists them under 'Ignored files'. If either
appears in the commit, a pattern is misspelled or the file was
already tracked, which `.gitignore` does not undo;
`git rm --cached <file>` untracks a file without deleting it.
The same check belongs before the first commit of every real
project.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Start a repository | `git init -b main` |
| See what changed | `git status`; `git diff`; `git diff --staged` |
| Commit one logical change | `git add <file>`; `git commit -m "Why"` |
| Read the history of a file | `git log -p <file>` |
| Experiment on a branch | `git switch -c <branch>`; `git merge <branch>` |
| Find leftover conflict markers | `git grep -n -e '<<<<<<<' -e '>>>>>>>'` |
| Create a private remote and push | `gh repo create <name> --private --source=. --remote=origin`; `git push -u origin main` |
| Tag a submission | `git tag -a v1.0 -m "..."`; `git push origin v1.0` |
| Look at a tagged version | `git switch --detach v1.0`; `git switch main` |
| Undo, safely | @tbl-git-solo-oh-no; `git reflog` first |

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-05}

1. Even for solo work, Git provides a time machine (roll back to
   any prior state), a branching workflow (try risky refactors
   without fear), a structured log of what you did, when, and why,
   and an off-site backup if you push to a remote. The cost is a
   one-time learning curve; the benefit compounds for the rest of
   your career, especially when 'solo' projects become
   collaborations.
2. A commit is a snapshot of the repository at a point in time,
   with a parent commit, an author, a message, and a unique hash.
   A branch is a movable pointer to a commit, used to develop
   features or experiments in isolation. A tag is an immovable
   pointer to a commit, used to mark release points (submissions,
   deployments). Commits are the units of history; branches are
   the units of parallel work; tags are the units of milestones.
3. You are in the middle of editing files but need to pull changes
   from the remote or switch to another branch urgently.
   `git stash` puts your uncommitted work temporarily aside;
   `git stash pop` restores it later. This avoids committing
   half-finished work just to unblock a branch switch. Once popped
   or dropped, a stash is no longer in any reflog; it can be found
   for a short time with `git fsck --no-reflogs --unreachable`, but
   anything that matters should be committed instead.
